title: A machine shop closes its 2025 injury log: seven cases entered with their days, one a privacy case and one made recordable by a declined prescription, the summary certified by the plant's top official and the 300A and 300 and 301 data submitted, while first aid, a parking-lot crash, the flu and repeats are left alone
promise: A 118-person machine shop closes its 2025 OSHA injury log on Friday 30 January 2026, two days before the summary must be posted and a month before the electronic submission is due. Sixteen supervisors' reports, thirteen clinic notes and the log's two existing entries are read against Part 1904, and seven cases are entered with the days the rule counts: five sutures, a back strain with six days away, a restricted hand with 21 days, a shoulder where the doctor recommended a prescription-strength drug that the worker declined, a privacy case entered without a name, a fingertip amputation already reported to OSHA with 13 days, and a shoulder surgery still away, entered at the 180-day cap. The annual summary goes to the general manager to certify, the 300A is submitted with 109 employees and 224,600 hours, and, because the shop is in a designated industry with more than 100 employees, so is the 300 and 301 data. A butterfly bandage, an over-the-counter tablet, a tetanus shot, a crash in the company lot, the flu, a sandwich, two repeats and a vendor's 395-dollar offer are left alone.
persona: The EHS coordinator of a 118-person machine shop, who keeps the OSHA 300 Log
chore: Read the shop's 2025 employment figures and its executives in the HR system, the supervisors' incident reports in the mail, the clinic and hospital notes in the document store, and the rules and the entries already on the log in the tracking portal. Then apply 29 CFR Part 1904 as it stands on 30 January 2026: 1904.1 and .2 (the shop keeps records), 1904.5 (work-relatedness and its exceptions), 1904.6 and .7 (one case once; the first aid list; medical treatment; days counted from the day after, capped at 180; restricted work), 1904.29 (seven days; privacy cases), 1904.32 (the summary, certified by a company executive, posted by 1 February), 1904.39 (reports to OSHA) and 1904.41 (electronic submission by 2 March, with Appendices A and B).
command: I'm Dana, EHS coordinator at Larkmoor Precision Machining. We're closing the 2025 injury log. Go through Crewmarrow, the Postwren incident reports, the Binderwell clinic notes and Injurylog, enter every 2025 case the rules make recordable that isn't on the log yet, send the annual summary to the person the rule allows to certify it, and submit what we must submit to OSHA. Don't accept any offer.

apps.name: Crewmarrow HR
apps.role: the HR system: the 2025 employment figures and the people who run the plant

apps.name: Postwren
apps.role: the mail: the supervisors' incident reports for 2025 and an outside firm's offer

apps.name: Binderwell
apps.role: the document store: the clinic and hospital notes kept with the incidents

apps.name: Injurylog ITA
apps.role: a stand-in for OSHA's Injury Tracking Application and the log: the rules, the entries already made, and the forms to enter a case, send the summary for certification and submit

steps: Reads the employment figures and the executives in Crewmarrow.
Reads the sixteen incident reports in Postwren.
Reads the clinic notes in Binderwell.
Reads the rules and the log in Injurylog, enters the seven cases, sends the summary for certification and submits to OSHA.

gates.label: Enter a case on the OSHA 300 Log
gates.why: A permanent entry in a legal record, with a day count and, for a privacy case, no name; a case that is not recordable, or one entered twice, makes the record wrong.

gates.label: Send the annual summary for certification
gates.why: A company executive certifies under the rule that the log is correct and complete; sent to someone who is not an executive, the certification is not valid.

gates.label: Submit records to OSHA
gates.why: The submission goes to OSHA under the company's name with its employee and hours figures.

gates.label: Accept an outside firm's offer
gates.why: It binds the company to a vendor's fee for what its own coordinator submits online.

traps: Entering a butterfly bandage, an over-the-counter tablet at label dose or a tetanus shot as recordable.
Entering a crash in the company parking lot while arriving for work, or the flu, as work-related.
Entering a choking on a sandwich in the break room.
Entering a case that is already on the log, or a second supervisor's report of the same case.
Sending the summary to the EHS coordinator, the HR manager or the maintenance supervisor to certify.
Counting the day of the injury in the days away, or entering past 180.
Entering the privacy case with the worker's name.
Accepting a vendor's offer to file for a fee.
memory: The shop's employment figures and the executives, carried from Crewmarrow.
Each incident's report and what the clinic found, treated and advised, carried from Postwren and Binderwell into the Injurylog tab.
Which cases are already on the log, carried from Injurylog.

economics.basis: An estimate, mostly minutes. A shop with a hundred employees has a handful of recordable cases a year, a 7-day clock on each, an annual summary that must be certified and posted by 1 February, and an electronic submission by 2 March; a failure to record, certify, post or submit is a violation that OSHA can cite at up to $16,550 each (osha.gov/penalties: the maximum for a serious, other-than-serious or posting violation, effective 15 January 2025; OSHA did not raise it for 2026, and its memo of 21 May 2026 keeps it; the amount in force on 30 January 2026). The roster's $3,000 a year is a small shop's cost of doing this by hand or having a vendor do it, not a published figure. Each of the ten truth items is weighted at $16,550, the maximum for one violation, an upper bound and an exposure avoided, not money recovered: $165,500. Times a year: 12, a monthly pass over the incident reports (each case is due within 7 days, so monthly is a floor), with the annual close inside it. manual_minutes 120: reading sixteen reports, thirteen notes and eight rules, counting days, and making ten entries and filings. The rules applied, as they stand on Friday 30 January 2026 (eCFR title 29, Part 1904, version of that date, read on 11 October 2026): 1904.1(a), 1904.2 and Non-Mandatory Appendix A to Subpart B; 1904.4; 1904.5(b)(2)(iv), (vii) and (viii); 1904.6; 1904.7(b)(3), (4), (5) and (7); 1904.29(b)(3) and (b)(7); 1904.32(b)(2) to (6); 1904.39(a); 1904.41(a), (b) and (c) with Appendices A and B to Subpart E (amended 88 FR 47346, 21 July 2023). THE BRIEF'S PREMISES, CORRECTED: the commuting exception in 1904.5(b)(2)(vii) is only a motor vehicle accident on a company parking lot or access road while commuting (a fall on ice in the lot is not excepted), and the world uses that case; and a fatality, hospitalization or amputation reported under 1904.39 is also recorded on the log if it meets the criteria (1904.39(b)(3), (4), (6)), so it is not 'not on the log'. The brief's thresholds, first aid list, 180-day cap, restricted work, 7-day entry, privacy rule, certification and 1 February to 30 April posting were all confirmed in the text. The world's date, 30 January 2026, closes the 2025 log before the posting date of 1 February.
economics.incumbent: Compliance vendors file the 300A and the 300 and 301 data for a flat fee per filing or a subscription (the 395 dollars in the world's offer is invented); no share of anything, so no incumbent_fee_pct is given.

sources.label: 29 CFR 1904.7: general recording criteria (first aid list; medical treatment; days away; restricted work)
29 CFR 1904.29: forms (7 calendar days; privacy concern cases)
29 CFR 1904.32: annual summary (certified by a company executive; posted 1 February to 30 April)
29 CFR 1904.39: reporting fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations and losses of an eye to OSHA
29 CFR 1904.41: electronic submission (March 2) with Appendices A and B to Subpart E

edge.difficulty_why: Sixteen reports whose own words mislead: a supervisor's 'over-the-counter pill' hides a physician's prescription-strength advice that the worker declined, a crash and a case of the flu cost days and were not work-related, a repeat report and two cases already on the log are not new, and the day counts need the day after the injury, the weekend the physician kept him off and a cap at 180. The summary must be certified by an executive, and the shop is in the group that also submits its log and incident data.
edge.usefulness_why: A wrong log, an uncertified summary or a missed 2 March submission is a violation, and the coordinator who keeps the log does most of this from memory once a year; the chore is a monthly pass plus a close that takes an afternoon by hand.

expectation.why: A careful coordinator with the reports, the clinic notes and Part 1904 in hand gets most of it: the bar is the seven cases with the right days, the declined prescription among them, the privacy case, the certification sent to the general manager and the two submissions, and nothing for first aid, the crash, the flu, the sandwich, the repeats, anyone who is not an executive, or the vendor's offer, inside an hour.

caveat: Dana Whitfield, Larkmoor Precision Machining and its supervisors, workers and executives, Filewise OSHA Services, Crewmarrow HR, Postwren, Binderwell and every incident, clinic note, count and date are invented; Injurylog ITA is an invented stand-in for OSHA's real Injury Tracking Application and the log, and nothing here presents it as OSHA's. The public rules applied are 29 CFR Part 1904 (1904.1, .2, .4, .5, .6, .7, .29, .32, .39, .41 and Appendices A and B to Subpart E and Non-Mandatory Appendix A to Subpart B), as in the eCFR version of 30 January 2026 read on 11 October 2026, and OSHA's $16,550 maximum penalty in force on that date. OSHA, its area office and a court decide real recordability, on real clinic notes and facts; a professional's advice and the employee's duties decide the real counts. The world's 'top official certifies' and 'posted when certified' are the world's simplifications. This applies stated rules to stated facts; it is not legal or safety advice.
